records.sourceFile: Considerations for Velocity Based Training - The instruction to move as fast as possible is less effective than a target velocity .pdf

paper.citation: Hirsch SM, Frost DM. Considerations for velocity-based training: the instruction to move "as fast as possible" is less effective than a target velocity. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019.
paper.abstract: The study compared two instructions during a free-weight bench press: reach a target velocity of 1.0 m/s, or move as fast as possible. Thirteen male powerlifters performed 4 sets of 5 repetitions at 45% 1RM under each instruction, and their repetitions to failure at 75% 1RM were then compared. The target-velocity instruction produced a faster best repetition per set, with no difference in the subsequent repetition test.
paper.tldr: Telling powerlifters to reach a challenging 1.0 m/s target produced slightly faster best-repetition bar speeds than telling them to move as fast as possible. The faster speeds did not reduce how many repetitions they completed in a later 75% 1RM set.
paper.methods: Thirteen male powerlifters (of 15 tested) completed two randomised sessions of 4 sets of 5 bench press repetitions at 45% 1RM, under either a 1.0 m/s target or move-as-fast-as-possible instruction, with feedback after each repetition from a linear position transducer. Mean velocity of each repetition was measured with a 3D motion capture system, and the fastest mean velocity per set was compared by a 2 x 4 repeated-measures ANOVA. The 75% 1RM repetition test was compared by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
paper.findings: The fastest mean velocity per set averaged 0.84 m/s with the target instruction and 0.82 m/s with the move-as-fast-as-possible instruction (p=0.0002). Eleven of 13 participants were faster under the target instruction, by about 0.03 m/s on average, and only one exceeded the 1.0 m/s target. Repetitions completed at 75% 1RM were 9.6 with the target instruction and 10.0 with the other instruction (p=0.43).
paper.limitations: Small sample of 13 male powerlifters, one exercise, one relative load and one target velocity. Only the fastest repetition of each set was analysed, and the authors state that using all repetitions may have shown no significant difference. The fixed target was not individualised and was out of reach for most participants. Acute velocity was measured, not training adaptations. The PDF states a 2019 publication year, while the Crossref record gives 2021; the PDF year is used here.
paper.practicalImplications: A challenging velocity target, even one most lifters did not reach, produced slightly faster best-repetition bar speeds during bench press sets at 45% 1RM than a move-as-fast-as-possible cue, without reducing repetitions in a later set in the same session. The authors suggest individualised targets may work better than one fixed target. Load-velocity estimates of 1RM taken under one cue may not transfer to the other.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches who monitor bar speed can try a challenging velocity target during bench press training to elicit faster best-repetition velocity. The effect was small (0.02 m/s on average) and was measured within one session with powerlifters only.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured athletes or return-to-sport testing, so it cannot be used to set velocity targets or judge readiness during rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Effects of four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance.pdf

paper.citation: Riscart-López J, Rendeiro-Pinho G, Mil-Homens P, Soares-daCosta R, Loturco I, Pareja-Blanco F, et al. Effects of four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020.
paper.abstract: Forty-three moderately strength-trained men were randomly assigned to linear, undulating, reverse or constant velocity-based training models and followed an 8-week full squat programme. The authors report that all groups trained at similar average relative intensity, velocity loss, number of sets and rest. All groups improved 1RM, velocity-related outcomes, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time, with no significant group by time interactions.
paper.tldr: Four different velocity-based squat programming models, with 20% velocity loss, 3 sets and 4 minutes of rest, produced similar gains in squat strength, jump height and sprint time in moderately trained men over 8 weeks. The time course of strength gains looked less pronounced in the undulating group, but no between-group difference was statistically significant.
paper.methods: Forty-six men were matched on 1RM and randomly assigned, and 43 completed an 8-week intervention of two sessions per week (linear n=11, undulating n=10, reverse n=11, constant n=11). Velocity was measured for every repetition with a linear velocity transducer, and loads were adjusted daily to the velocity-predicted %1RM. Pre- and post-tests included predicted 1RM, velocity at common loads, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time, analysed with a 4 x 2 ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: No significant group by time interactions were found for 1RM (p=0.18), velocity variables, countermovement jump (p=0.22) or sprint time (p=0.98). Within groups, 1RM rose significantly in all four groups (10.9% undulating to 18.0% reverse), with effect sizes of about 0.3 to 0.5 for jump height and 0.3 for sprint time. The constant group trained with a significantly slower average velocity and a higher mean relative intensity (about 67.5% vs 62.5% 1RM) than the other groups.
paper.limitations: Smith machine used for testing and training, which limits transfer to free-weight training. Sample was moderately trained recreational men (not elite athletes), training frequency was two sessions a week, and there was no non-training control group. The abstract states all groups trained with similar relative average intensity, but Table 2 shows the constant group trained at a higher mean relative intensity (p<0.001) and the undulating group did fewer repetitions per set at 50% 1RM. The PDF prints 2020 as the publication year, while the Crossref record gives 2021; the PDF year is used here.
paper.practicalImplications: In moderately trained men, a velocity-based squat programme using 20% velocity loss within sets, 3 sets and 4 minutes of rest produced similar strength and jump gains whichever loading model was used. Coaches can choose among these models for variety; the authors' observation that strength rose more slowly with undulating programming was not statistically significant and should not drive model choice on its own.
paper.athleteDev: Velocity-based squat programming with monitored velocity loss was followed by gains in strength and jump performance in moderately trained adults, though without a control group. The four programming models gave similar results, so selection can rest on the coach's preference or the timing of the training block.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured people or a return-to-sport outcome. It cannot be used to set loads or progressions during rehabilitation or to judge readiness to return to play.

records.sourceFile: Effects of low load resistance training with vascular     occlusion on the mechanical properties of muscle and tendon.pdf

paper.citation: Kubo K, Komuro T, Ishiguro N, Tsunoda N, Sato Y, Ishii N, et al. Effects of low-load resistance training with vascular occlusion on the mechanical properties of muscle and tendon. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2006;22:112-119.
paper.abstract: Nine participants trained one knee extensor with low load (20% of 1RM) and vascular occlusion and the other with high load (80% of 1RM) for 12 weeks, three days a week. Both protocols increased maximal isometric torque and muscle volume. Specific tension of the vastus lateralis and tendon-aponeurosis stiffness increased after high-load training but did not change after low-load occlusion training.
paper.tldr: Low-load training with vascular occlusion increased knee extensor strength and muscle volume in healthy young men, but unlike high-load training it did not significantly raise muscle specific tension, voluntary activation or tendon stiffness within the trained leg. Direct comparisons between the two methods were not significant, so the difference is suggestive rather than shown.
paper.methods: Nine healthy young men completed 12 weeks of unilateral knee extension, with each leg randomly assigned to low load (20% 1RM, 4 sets averaging 17.5 repetitions, 30 s rest, occlusion pressure raised every four weeks) or high load (80% 1RM, 4 sets of 10, 1 min rest). Outcomes were maximal isometric torque, muscle volume by 0.5 T MRI, voluntary activation by twitch interpolation, EMG, vastus lateralis specific tension, and tendon-aponeurosis and patella tendon stiffness by ultrasound. Data were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Maximal torque rose 7.8% with low-load occlusion training and 16.8% with high-load training, and quadriceps volume rose in both (reported as 5.9% and 7.4%, p=0.195 between protocols). Voluntary activation (3.2%), mEMG (20.5%), specific tension (5.5%) and tendon-aponeurosis stiffness (45.6 to 59.3 N/mm) rose only after high-load training. Patella tendon stiffness and cross-sectional area did not change with either protocol, and between-protocol differences in torque gain (p=0.107) and stiffness gain (p=0.131) were not significant.
paper.limitations: Only nine men were studied with one exercise and one 12-week programme, and both protocols were done in the same participants. Patella tendon elongation was not corrected for joint rotation, and specific tension used fascicle length during contraction rather than optimal length. The text reports muscle volume gains of 5.9% (low load) and 7.4% (high load), but Table 1 means (1892 to 2032 and 1878 to 2011 cm3) imply about 7.4% and 7.1%. The authors' suggestions that occlusion training could raise tendon injury risk or favour stretch-shortening performance were speculation and not tested.
paper.practicalImplications: In healthy young men, 12 weeks of low-load training with vascular occlusion increased strength and muscle volume, but significant changes in tendon stiffness, voluntary activation and specific tension were seen only after high-load training. Coaches who use occlusion training to build size and strength should not assume it reproduces the tendon and neural adaptations of heavy loading.
paper.athleteDev: This study gives mechanistic evidence that high-load training raised tendon stiffness, voluntary activation and specific tension while low-load occlusion training did not change them significantly. Because the between-protocol tests were not significant, it supports caution rather than a firm conclusion when tendon stiffness is a training goal.
paper.rtp: The study used healthy men and did not test injured tendons or any return-to-sport outcome. It cannot show that low-load occlusion training is safe or effective for rehabilitating a tendon, so it should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: How Do They Decide - Performance Support Staff Perceptions of Decision-Making in Elite-Sport Environments.pdf

paper.citation: Wilson PJ, Roe G, Kiely J. How Do They Decide? Performance Support Staff Perceptions of Decision-Making in Elite-Sport Environments. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.
paper.abstract: A mixed-methods online survey of 191 performance support staff in professional or international sport examined their views on decision-making, how they learn it and how they track decisions. Most rated decision-making as very important, but few had formal training or a formal review process, and staff described pressure, poor team communication and cognitive biases as obstacles.
paper.tldr: Performance staff rate decision-making as central to their role, yet most have no formal training and no structured way to review key decisions. The authors suggest starting with basic education on decision-making and cognitive bias, then adding a formal process for tracking and reviewing major decisions.
paper.methods: Nonprobability (purposive and snowball) recruitment over an 8-week period. An online questionnaire with nine decision-making items (eight closed, one open) and six demographic items was checked by a five-expert panel. Closed items were summarized descriptively, and the open item was analysed by thematic analysis.
paper.findings: Decision-making was rated 5 or higher by 98% of respondents (median 7). Ninety percent believed team decisions give better outcomes than individual decisions. Thirty-one percent had received formal decision-making education, 69% had no formal strategy for scoring key decisions, and 22% consistently reviewed and adjusted plans. Five themes emerged from the open responses: environmental pressures, lack of systems and processes, underdeveloped decision capabilities, dysfunctional team dynamics and cognitive biases.
paper.limitations: The authors note that the sample was recruited non-randomly, that only 12 respondents were women, and that the findings may not generalize to all professional sport. The survey did not measure the type of decision training received, and the preference for experiential over targeted training (median 3 on a 7-point scale) was not explored further. The PDF is dated 2024 while Crossref lists 2025, and the PDF year is used.
paper.practicalImplications: Organizations can start with basic education on decision-making and cognitive bias, then add a formal process for recording and reviewing major decisions. Team decision-making depends on trust and communication, which respondents named as barriers.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: staff who make training-load, selection or return-related calls can keep a simple log of key decisions and their outcomes and review it on a set schedule. The paper does not test whether this improves decision quality.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not test return-to-play decisions, but respondents described conflicts over return from injury around key games. Use the findings to review how return decisions are made and who is involved, not as evidence for a specific return protocol.

records.sourceFile: Ischemic strength training - a low load alternative to     heavy resistance exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Wernbom M, Augustsson J, Raastad T. Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports. 2008.
paper.abstract: The authors review the physiology, safety and dosing of strength training combined with vascular occlusion. They note that low-load occlusion training produces strength and size gains comparable to heavy training in several studies, but that mechanisms, long-term safety and practical use remain unclear. They suggest that relative ischemia may occur without a cuff at some loads.
paper.tldr: Low-load training with a tourniquet can build muscle and strength, but the mechanisms, long-term safety and practical dose are unresolved. Where heavy loads are contraindicated, it is an option, with wide cuffs at lower pressures preferred and attention to soreness and effort.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the authors' and published work on motor unit recruitment, hormonal and local growth factor responses, safety, cuff width and training dose. The authors summarize 13 training studies in Table 1, but no search strategy or inclusion criteria are described.
paper.findings: Low-load training with partial occlusion at about 20% to 50% of 1RM produced muscle size and strength gains comparable to heavy training in several studies. In one 12-week study, a low-load occlusion leg and a high-load leg gained similar quadriceps volume, but only the high-load leg increased tendon-aponeurosis stiffness and muscle activation. A Japanese survey of more than 12,600 occlusion-training users from 105 centers reported subcutaneous hemorrhage in 13.1% and rare serious events, including venous thrombosis in 0.055%.
paper.limitations: The authors state that long-term safety, soft-tissue effects, optimal frequency and whether cuffs add benefit beyond effort need further study. Several supporting points rest on unpublished observations, and one partial-occlusion cycling study (Eiken et al.) found an 8% fall in peak torque despite fiber-area gains.
paper.practicalImplications: If a cuff is used, the authors favor relatively wide cuffs at lower pressures, noting about 90 to 110 mm Hg was enough with a 135 mm cuff in their unpublished observations, rather than high pressures with narrow cuffs. Expect intense muscle pain and delayed soreness, which the authors say lessens with low starting volumes of 1 to 2 sets, and note that the training demands high motivation.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports low-load occlusion as a complement to strength work or when heavy loads are inappropriate. It does not show it beats heavy training for tendon or neural adaptation, so do not use it to replace heavy lifting for strength-focused athletes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review positions occlusion training for rehabilitation when heavy forces are contraindicated, but it gives no return-to-play criteria and cites no trials in injured athletes. Low-load occlusion did not increase tendon stiffness in the one study that measured it, which matters when tendon loading is a rehab goal.

records.sourceFile: Managing Fatigue in Team Sports - A Brief Review of Concurrent Training Effects Within the Microcycle.pdf

paper.citation: Grammenou M, Nulty CD. Managing Fatigue in Team Sports: A Brief Review of Concurrent Training Effects Within the Microcycle. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2025;47(5):589-600.
paper.abstract: Concurrent training, which combines resistance exercise and energy-system conditioning, is the default approach for high-intensity intermittent team sports. This review explains the complexities of concurrent training for fatigue management and offers simplified recommendations for adjusting training variables within a microcycle. It also addresses travel, sleep and nutrition, which affect fatigue during congested competition periods.
paper.tldr: A narrative review for team sport strength and conditioning staff on scheduling resistance and high-intensity conditioning in a congested week. Intensity, volume, session order, travel, sleep and protein intake are the main levers, and the decision tree is a starting point rather than a prescription.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The paper does not describe a systematic search or study selection process. It draws on cited studies, including a meta-analysis on minimum effective resistance dose, and on practical experience.
paper.findings: The review suggests that high-intensity resistance work (above about 80% 1RM or fewer than 8 repetitions) is a minimum threshold for maximal strength gains, and that its recovery demands can interfere with later sessions. It cites evidence that as few as one set per exercise, three times a week at 70-85% 1RM, can improve strength in trained athletes, and suggests about 12 weekly sets per muscle group as a reasonable volume. It reports that strength work before low-intensity aerobic work may give better outcomes, while data on high-intensity endurance sessions are limited. It recommends protein intake of about 1.2-1.7 g/kg/day and spaced post-exercise protein, and advises sleep hygiene and planning for travel-related circadian disruption.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were chosen, and its recommendations are described by the authors as guidelines, not prescriptions. The text states that there is no direct research on the combined effects of sleep disruption and travel on concurrent training, that the cohorts in the interference literature likely have lower training age and weekly demands than team sport athletes, and that molecular interference has been observed mostly in the lower body.
paper.practicalImplications: When planning a congested microcycle, match resistance intensity and volume to the competition load, and consider limiting sets taken close to failure before high-speed or conditioning sessions that need to be fresh. Use velocity loss, RPE or RIR to control volume where available. If strength is the priority, the review suggests scheduling strength work before low-intensity aerobic work. Track sleep and protein intake alongside training load, since the review links both to recovery from concurrent training.
paper.athleteDev: Use the decision tree (Figure 3) as a starting point to adjust resistance intensity, volume, session order and recovery across the microcycle as competition load changes. Protect sleep and protein intake during congested periods, since the review links both to recovery from combined strength and conditioning work.
paper.rtp: The review is written for healthy team sport athletes and gives no rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria. It mentions return from injury only as a time window in which strength work could be prioritized. It cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to return or to set tolerance tests.

records.sourceFile: Position-Specific Longitudinal Assessment of Total and Regional Body Composition in NCAA Division I Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Brooks SG, Dengel DR. Position-Specific Longitudinal Assessment of Total and Regional Body Composition in NCAA Division I Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.
paper.abstract: The study examined preseason to postseason changes in total and regional body composition by position in 188 NCAA Division I football players, measured by DXA. Total body mass, fat mass and bone mass were largely stable, but lean mass fell in several position groups, mainly in the legs and gynoid region. Muscle-to-bone ratios also decreased in several positions.
paper.tldr: Lean mass in Division I football players fell during the competitive season in most position groups, mainly in the legs and the gynoid region (hips and upper thighs). Total body mass and fat mass were stable.
paper.methods: A retrospective longitudinal study used DXA scans taken at preseason and postseason from 2019 to 2023, with one scan pair per player. Two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA tested the effects of season and position, with playing status as a covariate, and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons were used to test within-position changes.
paper.findings: Total lean mass decreased within defensive backs (76.17 to 75.12 kg), offensive linemen (104.00 to 102.30 kg), punters/kickers, running backs, tight ends and wide receivers, but not in defensive linemen, linebackers or quarterbacks. Leg lean mass decreased in all positions except linebackers and quarterbacks, gynoid lean mass fell in all positions except quarterbacks, and total mass and fat mass did not change. Total muscle-to-bone ratio fell in defensive backs, defensive linemen, tight ends and wide receivers.
paper.limitations: The PDF prints the year 2025, while the Crossref record lists 2026; the PDF year is used here. The paper has internal inconsistencies: age SD is 1.6 in the abstract but 1.4 in Table 1, the Discussion says total lean mass fell in every position except linebackers and quarterbacks while Results and Table 2 show no change in defensive linemen, and some table rows look duplicated (arm lean mass equals total bone mineral content). The design is a single season with no nutrition, training, injury or performance data, and several position groups are small.
paper.practicalImplications: Body composition monitoring by position can show where lean mass is being lost during a season, and the authors point to the legs and gynoid region. Staff could use DXA or similar repeated measures to tailor lower-body resistance training and nutrition for individual players, though the study does not show that these steps prevent the loss.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Repeated preseason and postseason body composition checks can show whether a player is losing lower-body lean mass, which is the main regional change in this cohort. The authors suggest emphasising lower-body resistance training and maintaining lean mass in season for positions that rely on explosive movement, though the study does not test this.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Players injured for the season appear only as a covariate category, and the paper reports no injury outcomes, rehabilitation or return-to-play data.

records.sourceFile: Rapid increase in plasma growth hormone after low     intensity resistance exercise with vascular occlusion.pdf

paper.citation: Takarada Y, Nakamura Y, Aruga S, Onda T, Miyazaki S, Ishii N. Rapid increase in plasma growth hormone after low-intensity resistance exercise with vascular occlusion. J Appl Physiol. 2000;88(1):61-65.
paper.abstract: Six young male athletes did five sets of knee extension at about 20% of 1RM to exhaustion, with and without a thigh pressure cuff. Growth hormone, norepinephrine and lactate rose markedly only when the cuff was used.
paper.tldr: Very light resistance exercise (about 20% of 1RM) with blood-flow occlusion produced a large growth hormone rise in six young men, while the same work without the cuff did not. The study measured hormones and muscle activity in one session and no training outcome, so it cannot show that this method builds muscle.
paper.methods: Six young male athletes performed bilateral seated leg extensions with a pressure tourniquet on both thighs (214 mmHg) and, one week later, the same movement without occlusion, matched for intensity and repetitions. Each session was five sets to exhaustion at about 20% of 1RM with 30 s rest. Blood was drawn before exercise, immediately after, and at 15, 45 and 90 min and 24 h to measure lactate, GH, norepinephrine, IL-6, lipid peroxide and CPK, and vastus lateralis EMG was recorded; the two sessions were compared with paired t-tests.
paper.findings: Lactate, norepinephrine and GH rose sharply after the occluded session and changed little after the control session. GH peaked at 15 min at about 40 ug/l, roughly 290 times resting, which the authors state was about 1.7 times the rise they cite for high-intensity short-rest training. IL-6 rose gradually and stayed above control at 24 h, CPK and lipid peroxide did not differ significantly, and integrated EMG per concentric action was about 1.8 times higher with occlusion (P < 0.01).
paper.limitations: The sample was six men, and the text gives no effect size or power estimate. The abstract gives the intensity as about 20% of 1RM, but Table 1 shows a mean of 23.2 +/- 5.2% 1RM, ranging from 33.2% in set 1 to 15.5% in set 5; the table values are reported here. The control session was a week later and the text does not state whether session order was randomized. Only acute responses were measured, and the authors could not rule out microdamage or thrombosis risk in vessels.
paper.practicalImplications: Occlusion work at very light loads produced a strong acute hormonal and muscle activity response in young men, which makes it a candidate for a supervised test with athletes who cannot tolerate heavy loads. The study does not show that this response leads to muscle growth or strength gain, and the authors' long-term claims rest on unpublished observations.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes who cannot lift heavy loads, the study suggests very light occlusion work may produce a large acute GH and EMG response at about 20% of 1RM. Treat it as an unproven option: there are no training outcomes, and the authors could not rule out vascular microdamage.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It used young male athletes and measured no injury or rehabilitation outcomes; the discussion mentions earlier occlusion work after ACL reconstruction, but this paper did not test injured or rehabilitating athletes.

records.sourceFile: Strength training - In search of optimal strategies to maximize neuromuscular performance.pdf

paper.citation: Duchateau J, Stragier S, Baudry S, Carpentier A. Strength training: in search of optimal strategies to maximize neuromuscular performance. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews. 2020. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Low-load training under blood-flow restriction (BFR) can increase muscle size and maximal strength about as well as heavy-load training, but it produces only minor neural adaptations. The authors propose protocols that combine high voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
paper.tldr: Low-load BFR training builds size and strength but adds little neural adaptation and may not be enough for well-trained athletes. The paper argues for combining high mechanical tension with metabolic stress, for example through brief inter-set rests, but this needs testing in more groups.
paper.methods: Perspective-style narrative review. The authors compare high-load training with low-load BFR training, discuss the mechanisms of hypertrophy and neural adaptation, summarise meta-analyses, and present their own 3/7 method studies against comparison protocols.
paper.findings: Two meta-analyses (one in musculoskeletal patients, one in mixed populations) found smaller strength gains with low-load BFR than with high-load training, about 7% smaller in the latter, while a third with stricter inclusion criteria found no difference; hypertrophy differed by less than 1%. In the authors' 12-week elbow flexor study in moderately trained people, the 3/7 method raised 1RM by 22.2% versus 12.1% for 8x6, and biceps thickness by 9.6% versus 5.5%. Low-load BFR training produces only minor neural adaptations, and the mechanisms of its hypertrophy effect remain unresolved.
paper.limitations: The narrative format means the literature selection cannot be checked, and the paper leans on the authors' own studies, whose sample sizes are not given in the text. In the bench press study, 8x6 produced a larger 1RM gain (35.9%) and peak power gain (21.6% versus 16.3%) than 3/7, so the 3/7 advantage holds only against volume-matched or reverse-order protocols. Figure 3 is a hypothetical model. Crossref lists 2021, but the PDF prints 2020 on the copyright line and marks the article as published ahead of print, so 2020 is kept. No volume or page numbers are printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Low-load BFR training looks usable for patients and for sedentary or older adults, but the paper judges it likely insufficient for well-trained athletes who need high strength or power. For athletes, the authors suggest alternating high-load and low-load BFR work, using moderate-to-high loads with brief inter-set rests, or periodising complementary methods, and say well-designed studies are still needed to choose between them.
paper.athleteDev: For strength coaches, the paper suggests that well-trained athletes should not rely on low-load BFR alone for maximal strength. It offers moderate loads (about 70% 1RM) with brief rests (the 3/7 method, about 1.5 min per exercise bout) as a time-efficient option, while noting that a higher-volume 8x6 protocol gave larger 1RM gains in one study. Test any new protocol on your own athletes first, since the 3/7 evidence comes from active and moderately trained people.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its rehabilitation content is limited to the statement that low-load BFR training is valid and safe for frail and sarcopenic patients, which does not set return-to-play criteria for athletes. Do not use the BFR evidence to set post-injury loading targets for athletes.

records.sourceFile: The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical responses to resistance exercise - A mini review.pdf

paper.citation: Wilk M, Tufano JJ, Zajac A. The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise: A Mini Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(8):2369-2383.
paper.abstract: This mini review examines how movement tempo, the duration of each phase of a repetition, changes the acute responses to resistance exercise. Slower tempos reduce the 1RM, the load that can be used and the number of repetitions performed, while increasing time under tension and affecting cardiovascular and hormonal responses. The authors advise coaches to test maximal strength and repetitions at each tempo used.
paper.tldr: Slower repetition tempos lower the load and number of repetitions a lifter can complete, and they increase total time under tension. Hormone, lactate and muscle damage responses to tempo are inconsistent, so coaches should test 1RM and maximal reps at the tempos they plan to use.
paper.methods: Mini review with a described keyword search of Google Scholar, MEDLINE, ADONIS, ERIC, SPORTDiscus, EBSCOhost and PubMed. Included studies were original, peer-reviewed, English-language studies of healthy adults using isotonic resistance exercise. The text gives no search dates, study counts, quality appraisal or pooled analysis.
paper.findings: Slower tempos reduced the maximal number of repetitions at a given load. For example, Headley et al. found that 2/0/2/0 gave 6.4 repetitions against 4.7 for 4/0/2/0 at 75% 1RM, and 1RM was 3.7% lower with the 4/0/2/0 tempo. Total time under tension rose with slower tempos, even when total repetitions fell. Post-exercise blood lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses differed between studies, and several studies found no difference. EMG and RPE findings were mixed across studies, two blood pressure studies found no clear tempo effect (load drove blood pressure in one), and the single muscle damage study found greater creatine kinase and soreness with a 4-second than a 1- or 2-second eccentric.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no pooled effect sizes or formal risk-of-bias assessment, so selection and weighting of studies cannot be checked. Most included studies were small acute experiments with different loads, exercises and tempo notation, and few isolated concentric or eccentric duration. The authors note that sex differences in tempo responses have not been studied empirically.
paper.practicalImplications: Test 1RM and maximal repetitions at each tempo used, because a slower tempo lowers the load and number of repetitions a lifter can manage. Track time under tension alongside repetitions when setting training volume, since slower tempos raise time under tension even when repetitions fall. The authors suggest varying tempo across sessions or within sets to reduce monotony, and say that without tempo-specific testing, tempo programming is trial and error.
paper.athleteDev: Treat tempo as a planned variable: a slower eccentric phase increases time under tension and requires lower loads, while a faster or explosive concentric suits power work. The review suggests slower tempos may be more activity-specific for sports that need long periods of constant tension, such as wrestling, but it does not measure sport performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review suggests that a variable or slower tempo may help injured athletes who cannot yet lift heavy loads or move explosively, because each phase can be controlled at lower loads. It includes no return-to-sport outcomes or criteria, so it cannot set return-to-sport readiness or load thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Velocity-based resistance training - Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response.pdf

paper.citation: Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Pareja-Blanco F, Ravelo-García AG, Ribas-Serna J, et al. Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism. 2020.
paper.abstract: Compared 10% and 30% velocity loss per set in an 8-week full-squat velocity-based program in 25 young men, measuring strength, jump, sprint, fatigue, knee extensor EMG, resting hormones and troponin T.
paper.tldr: In physically active men, sets stopped at 10% velocity loss produced strength and jump gains similar to sets at 30%, with under half the repetitions. Only the 10% group improved sprint times, and troponin T rose in both groups, more in the 30% group.
paper.methods: Randomized two-group, 8-week study. Participants were matched on estimated 1RM and randomly assigned. Both groups trained the full squat at 70-85% 1RM, three sets per session, twice weekly, with each set ended at 10% velocity loss or at a loss that progressed from 20% to 30% (average 29.4%). Pre and post tests included a 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, a progressive loading test with estimated 1RM, a fatigue test, knee extensor EMG and resting blood hormones.
paper.findings: Compliance was 100%. Both groups improved estimated 1RM (VL10% +17.9%, VL30% +14.9%) and fatigue-test repetitions (+74.8% and +73.2%). Countermovement jump rose 9.2% in the 10% group and 5.4% in the 30% group, with a small, non-significant between-group effect (0.23). Sprint times for 10 m and 20 m improved only in the 10% group (-1.6% and -1.5%), with a significant time-by-group interaction. EMG changes were not significant in either group. Troponin T rose 59.9% (10%) and 128.4% (30%), significant within both groups; no other resting hormone changed significantly.
paper.limitations: 1RM was estimated from bar velocity rather than measured, and there was no untrained control group. The abstract says only the 10% group showed EMG increments, but the Results report no significant EMG change in either group. The Results state troponin T changes were significantly greater in the 30% group, yet also state there was no significant time-by-group interaction for any biochemical marker. The 10% group repetition total is given as 109.6 plus or minus 2.0 in the Results and plus or minus 12.0 in the Discussion. The PDF is an accepted manuscript with only a 2020 download stamp and no volume, issue or pages.
paper.practicalImplications: Stopping sets at a set velocity loss is a practical way to control fatigue in a 70-85% 1RM squat program. Sets ended at 10% loss gave strength and fatigue-test gains similar to 30% loss with fewer repetitions and better sprint changes, so lower velocity-loss limits may suit programs that prioritize sprint and jump performance. This needs confirmation in trained athletes and with multi-exercise programs.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample of active men, a 10% velocity-loss set (about 2 to 3 repetitions in practice) gave strength and fatigue-test gains similar to a 30% set, with only the 10% group improving sprint time, using about half the repetitions. Coaches could use velocity loss as a set-ending rule, but the study was short, used non-athletes, and did not measure sport performance.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested injury-free men in a laboratory training block and included no injured or rehabilitating participants.
